summary: How cells respond to stress: they adapt, get injured, die by necrosis or apoptosis, collect pigments or deposits, or turn neoplastic. The skin is a handy place to see all of these, and the exam asks you to match a change to its mechanism and its setting.

points: Hypertrophy: bigger cells, more structural protein; seen in cells that cannot divide (cardiac and skeletal muscle).
Hyperplasia: more cells, from stem cell or mature cell division; callus is epidermal hyperplasia from friction.
Atrophy: smaller cells from less protein synthesis plus ubiquitin-proteasome breakdown and autophagy.
Metaplasia: one mature cell type replaced by another better able to handle stress, by reprogramming stem cells.
Squamous metaplasia of bronchi in smokers; intestinal columnar metaplasia of the esophagus in Barrett esophagus.
Metaplasia and pathologic hyperplasia (endometrial hyperplasia from unopposed estrogen) can progress to dysplasia and carcinoma; benign prostatic hyperplasia does not.
ATP depletion stops the Na+/K+ ATPase, so sodium and water enter and the cell swells.
Anaerobic glycolysis builds lactic acid; low pH clumps chromatin.
Ribosomes detach from rough ER, so protein synthesis falls.
Calcium influx activates phospholipases, proteases, endonucleases, and ATPases, and opens the mitochondrial permeability transition pore.
Reactive oxygen species cause lipid peroxidation of membranes, protein oxidation, and DNA breaks.
Reversible: swelling, fatty change, membrane blebbing, ER dilation, ribosome detachment.
Irreversible: plasma membrane rupture (enzymes such as troponin leak into blood), lysosomal rupture, amorphous mitochondrial densities, pyknosis, karyorrhexis, karyolysis.
Intrinsic path: DNA damage or loss of survival signals lets BAX and BAK open the outer mitochondrial membrane; BCL-2 normally blocks this.
Cytochrome c leaves the mitochondrion, binds APAF-1, and activates caspase-9.
Extrinsic path: Fas ligand binds Fas (CD95) or TNF binds TNF receptor 1, recruiting adaptor proteins that activate caspase-8.
Cytotoxic T cells use perforin to let granzyme B into the target, where it activates caspases directly.
Executioner caspases 3 and 7 finish the job in all three routes.
Apoptosis: cell shrinks, chromatin condenses, apoptotic bodies form and are eaten, membrane stays intact, no inflammation.
Necrosis: cell swells, membrane ruptures, contents leak, inflammation follows.
Lipofuscin: yellow-brown wear and tear pigment from lipid peroxidation, in aging heart, liver, and neurons.
Hemosiderin: golden-brown iron storage pigment that stains blue with Prussian blue; seen in bruises and iron overload.
Melanin (made from tyrosine in melanocytes) and bilirubin (from heme breakdown, seen as jaundice) are the other key endogenous pigments.
Exogenous pigments: inhaled carbon in lung macrophages and hilar nodes (anthracosis); tattoo ink held for life in dermal macrophages.
Dystrophic calcification: in dead or damaged tissue with normal serum calcium (atheromas, damaged valves, caseous necrosis, psammoma bodies).
Metastatic calcification: in normal tissue when serum calcium or phosphate is high (hyperparathyroidism, chronic kidney disease, vitamin D excess); favors lung, kidney, gastric mucosa, and vessels.
Infiltrates: fat in hepatocytes (steatosis, from alcohol or obesity); cholesterol in macrophages (foam cells in atheromas, skin and tendon xanthomas).
Amyloid: misfolded protein in beta-pleated sheets; Congo red stain shows apple-green birefringence under polarized light.
Benign: well differentiated, slow, often encapsulated, no invasion, no metastasis.
Anaplasia: pleomorphism, large dark nuclei, high nuclear to cytoplasmic ratio, prominent nucleoli, atypical mitoses, tumor giant cells.
Metastasis is the one feature that proves a tumor is malignant.
Dysplasia is disordered growth with loss of orientation; carcinoma in situ is full-thickness dysplasia with an intact basement membrane.
Grade describes how differentiated the cells look; stage (TNM) describes size and spread and predicts outcome better.

Hallmarks include oncogene signaling (BRAF V600E in melanoma), two-hit loss of RB and TP53, BCL-2 overexpression, telomerase, VEGF angiogenesis, invasion, Warburg aerobic glycolysis, and immune evasion (PD-L1).

rows: Myocardial infarct, ischemia of solid organs (not brain)
Cell outlines preserved, eosinophilic cells without nuclei
Tissue digested by enzymes into fluid
Cheese-like, granular debris inside a granuloma
Lipase frees fatty acids that bind calcium (saponification), chalky white
Bright pink immune complexes and fibrin in vessel walls

rows: Holds E2F, blocking G1 to S until CDK4/6 and cyclin D phosphorylate it
Both copies lost (two hits), cell cycle runs free
Senses DNA damage; p21 arrests G1, BAX triggers apoptosis

tricks.label: Shrink versus swell
tricks.text: Apoptosis shrinks the cell and stays quiet; necrosis swells the cell, bursts it, and calls in inflammation.

tricks.label: Dystrophic means dead
tricks.text: Dystrophic calcification lands on dead or damaged tissue with normal blood calcium. Metastatic calcification lands on normal tissue because blood calcium or phosphate is high.

tricks.label: Grade is the look, stage is the spread
tricks.text: Grade comes from the microscope (differentiation). Stage comes from the whole patient (size, nodes, metastasis) and matters more for prognosis.

highYield: Brain infarcts undergo liquefactive necrosis; infarcts of the heart, kidney, and spleen undergo coagulative necrosis.
Irreversible injury is marked by membrane damage and the nuclear changes pyknosis, karyorrhexis, and karyolysis.
Cytochrome c plus APAF-1 activates caspase-9 (intrinsic); Fas or TNF activates caspase-8 (extrinsic).
Prussian blue stains hemosiderin; Congo red with apple-green birefringence identifies amyloid.
Tattoo pigment persists because dermal macrophages hold it and do not carry it away.
Carcinoma in situ has not crossed the basement membrane, so it cannot metastasize.
BRAF V600E is the classic activating mutation in melanoma and common nevi.
pitfalls: Fatty change and cell swelling are reversible; do not call a cell dead until you see membrane rupture or nuclear breakdown.
Apoptosis also shows pyknosis, but without swelling or inflammation; the setting and the inflammation tell them apart.
Metaplasia is reversible and is not dysplasia; it is the soil in which dysplasia can grow.
Melanoma, lymphoma, mesothelioma, and seminoma end in -oma yet are malignant.

dumps.p: Draw a flowchart starting from low oxygen in a cell. Show how ATP loss leads to reversible changes and then to irreversible injury.
l: Low oxygen stops oxidative phosphorylation, ATP falls
Na+/K+ ATPase fails, sodium and water enter, cell and ER swell
Anaerobic glycolysis makes lactic acid, pH falls, chromatin clumps
Ribosomes detach, protein synthesis drops, fat accumulates
Calcium enters and activates phospholipases, proteases, and endonucleases
Mitochondrial permeability transition, more ATP loss and cytochrome c release
Membrane rupture and lysosomal enzyme leak mark irreversible injury
Nucleus shows pyknosis, karyorrhexis, karyolysis

dumps.p: Draw the intrinsic, extrinsic, and cytotoxic T cell routes to apoptosis side by side and label the key proteins in each.
l: Intrinsic trigger: DNA damage via p53 or loss of growth factor signals
BAX and BAK open the outer mitochondrial membrane; BCL-2 blocks them
Cytochrome c binds APAF-1, activates caspase-9
Extrinsic: Fas ligand to Fas, or TNF to TNF receptor 1, activates caspase-8
Cytotoxic T cell: perforin pore lets granzyme B in, granzyme activates caspases
All routes converge on caspases 3 and 7
Result: shrinkage, chromatin condensation, apoptotic bodies, no inflammation

summary: Healthy skin keeps microbes out with a dry, acidic, shedding surface and a crowd of harmless resident organisms. Infections start when that barrier breaks, and the depth the organism reaches names the disease. The exam also tests toxin-driven skin disease and which host problems invite which organism.

points: Staphylococcus epidermidis: the most common skin resident; coagulase negative.
Cutibacterium acnes: anaerobic gram-positive rod living deep in pilosebaceous units.
Corynebacterium (diphtheroids) in moist areas; Malassezia yeasts in oily, sebaceous areas.
Staphylococcus aureus is carried in the anterior nares by roughly a third of people, a source of later skin infection.
Stratum corneum is a dry, tight physical barrier.
Acidic surface (pH about 4.5 to 5.5) slows growth of many pathogens.
Sebum triglycerides are broken down to free fatty acids that are toxic to many bacteria.
Constant desquamation sheds organisms stuck to surface cells.
Keratinocytes and sweat make antimicrobial peptides: beta-defensins, cathelicidin (LL-37), and dermcidin.
Resident flora compete for nutrients and attachment sites (colonization resistance).
Entry through a breach: cut, bite, burn, fissure, insect bite, catheter, or injection.
Adherence: bacterial adhesins bind fibronectin, collagen, or other matrix proteins.
Colonization and invasion: spreading factors (hyaluronidase, streptokinase, DNases) loosen tissue.
Spread through tissue planes or lymphatics; damage comes from toxins and from the host's own inflammation.
Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome: exfoliative toxins A and B are proteases that cleave desmoglein 1.
The split is high in the epidermis (stratum granulosum); Nikolsky sign is positive and mucosa is spared because desmoglein 3 holds it together.
Toxin is made at a distant site (nose, umbilicus), so the blisters are sterile; infants and people with kidney failure clear toxin poorly.
Superantigens (TSST-1, streptococcal pyrogenic exotoxins) bind MHC class II and the T cell receptor V-beta region outside the peptide groove.
This activates up to about a fifth of all T cells, releasing a cytokine storm (IL-2, TNF, IFN-gamma) with fever, diffuse red rash, shock, and later desquamation of palms and soles.
Diabetes: neuropathy hides wounds, vascular disease limits blood flow, and hyperglycemia weakens neutrophils; foot infections are often polymicrobial.
Venous insufficiency and lymphedema leave protein-rich fluid that clears bacteria poorly, causing recurrent streptococcal cellulitis.
Tinea pedis fissures between toes are a common entry point for leg cellulitis.
Injection drug use: S aureus, including MRSA, abscesses at injection sites.
Neutropenia: Pseudomonas (ecthyma gangrenosum) and molds; pus may be scant.
T cell deficiency (HIV, transplant): severe HSV and VZV, extensive molluscum, mucocutaneous Candida.

charts.title: Depth of infection
rows: Raised, bright red, sharply demarcated border
S pyogenes or mixed aerobes and anaerobes
Pain out of proportion, rapid spread, crepitus, numb skin

charts.title: Host context and likely organism
rows: Leg cellulitis with lymphedema or venous stasis
Group A or other beta-hemolytic streptococci
Mixed: S aureus, streptococci, gram-negative rods, anaerobes
T cell deficiency with chronic oral and skin plaques
T cell deficiency with widespread vesicles

tricks.label: Depth ladder
tricks.text: Climb down the skin: impetigo (epidermis), erysipelas (upper dermis), cellulitis (deep dermis and fat), necrotizing fasciitis (fascia). The deeper it goes, the less defined the border and the sicker the patient.

tricks.label: Desmoglein 1 sits high
tricks.text: Desmoglein 1 is the main desmoglein of the upper epidermis, so cutting it splits the skin high. Mucosa also has plenty of desmoglein 3, so it stays intact.

highYield: S epidermidis is the most common normal skin organism; C acnes lives in hair follicles.
Erysipelas has a sharp raised border because it sits in the upper dermis and lymphatics.
Exfoliative toxin cleaves desmoglein 1, splitting the stratum granulosum in scalded skin syndrome.
Superantigens link MHC class II to T cell receptor V-beta without antigen processing.
Recurrent leg cellulitis follows lymphedema, venous insufficiency, and tinea pedis fissures.
Neutropenic patients get Pseudomonas skin infection (ecthyma gangrenosum).
pitfalls: Scalded skin syndrome blisters are sterile because toxin, not bacteria, reaches the skin; culture the source, not the blister.
Scalded skin syndrome spares mucosa and splits in the granular layer; toxic epidermal necrolysis involves mucosa and causes full-thickness necrosis.
Erysipelas versus cellulitis: sharp edge and raised border point to erysipelas; a vague edge points to deeper cellulitis.

dumps.p: Draw a cross section of skin from stratum corneum to fascia. Label the infection that occurs at each level and its usual organism.
l: Epidermis: impetigo, S aureus or S pyogenes
Hair follicle: folliculitis, S aureus
Upper dermis and lymphatics: erysipelas, S pyogenes
Deep dermis and subcutaneous fat: cellulitis, streptococci and S aureus
Walled-off pus in dermis or subcutis: abscess, S aureus
Fascia: necrotizing fasciitis, S pyogenes or mixed flora
Note the border gets less distinct as depth increases

dumps.p: List every way normal skin keeps pathogens out, and for each one, name a condition that breaks it.
l: Stratum corneum barrier: broken by cuts, burns, eczema
Acidic pH: raised by soaps or occlusion
Sebum free fatty acids: low before puberty, one reason tinea capitis is a childhood infection
Desquamation sheds attached microbes
Antimicrobial peptides: defensins, cathelicidin, dermcidin
Resident flora compete; broad-spectrum antibiotics remove them
Immune cells: neutropenia and T cell defects remove the second line

summary: Skin wounds heal in a fixed order: clot, inflammation, granulation tissue, then remodeling into a scar. This unit covers what speeds or stalls that process, abnormal scars, and the special injuries from burns, electricity, radiation, pressure, and brown recluse venom.

points: Hemostasis (minutes): vasoconstriction, platelet plug, and fibrin clot; platelets release PDGF and TGF-beta.
Inflammation (days 1 to 3): neutrophils arrive first, then macrophages dominate by about day 3 and clear debris and release growth factors.
Proliferation (about day 3 to week 3): granulation tissue of fibroblasts, new capillaries (VEGF), and type III collagen; keratinocytes migrate to cover the gap.
Remodeling (weeks to a year): type III collagen is replaced by type I; zinc-dependent matrix metalloproteinases reshape the matrix.
Strength is about 10 percent of normal at 1 week and plateaus at about 70 to 80 percent by 3 months.
Primary intention: clean wound with edges brought together; little granulation tissue and a thin scar.
Secondary intention: large gap; more inflammation, much more granulation tissue, and contraction by myofibroblasts.
Delayed healing: infection (most common local cause), diabetes, ischemia, glucocorticoids, malnutrition, foreign bodies, and movement or pressure.
Vitamin C is a cofactor for prolyl and lysyl hydroxylase; without it collagen cannot form stable triple helices.
Zinc is a cofactor for matrix metalloproteinases and for cell proliferation.
Glucocorticoids blunt inflammation and collagen synthesis, giving weak scars.
Only partial-thickness and full-thickness burns count toward burned surface area.
Hypovolemic burn shock: capillary leak moves plasma out of vessels in the first 24 to 48 hours.
Infection: Pseudomonas aeruginosa is the classic cause of burn wound sepsis.
Hypermetabolism: catecholamines, cortisol, and glucagon raise energy use and break down muscle.
Inhalation injury: facial burns, singed nasal hair, soot, hoarseness; carbon monoxide and cyanide poisoning.
Late: contractures over joints and squamous cell carcinoma in a chronic burn scar (Marjolin ulcer).
Skin resists current, so entry and exit wounds look small, but current runs along nerves, vessels, and muscle and heats deep tissue.
Deep muscle necrosis causes compartment syndrome and rhabdomyolysis; myoglobin in urine injures the kidney.
Alternating current tends to cause ventricular fibrillation; lightning tends to cause asystole and cardiac arrest.
Lightning can leave Lichtenberg figures: branching, fern-like red skin marks that fade within about a day.
Ionizing radiation breaks DNA directly and, more often, through hydroxyl radicals made from water.
Acute radiation dermatitis: erythema, then dry and moist desquamation; chronic: atrophy, telangiectasia, fibrosis, and obliterative endarteritis.
Years later: basal cell and squamous cell carcinoma, and angiosarcoma in the radiation field.

notes.h: Pressure, ear trauma, and spider bites
points: Pressure over bony prominences (sacrum, ischial tuberosities, greater trochanters, heels) above capillary pressure causes ischemia; shear tears deep vessels.
Muscle is more sensitive to ischemia than skin, so damage under the surface is often worse than it looks.

Cauliflower ear: blunt trauma causes a hematoma that lifts the perichondrium off cartilage; avascular cartilage loses its blood supply, dies, and is replaced by fibrous tissue and irregular new cartilage.
Brown recluse venom contains sphingomyelinase D, which damages cell membranes and triggers complement, neutrophils, and small-vessel thrombosis.
The bite becomes a red, white, and blue lesion with a central necrotic ulcer; systemic hemolysis is rare.

charts.title: Burn depth
rows: Blisters, white or mottled, blanches poorly
White, leathery, or charred; no blanching

charts.title: Abnormal scars and wound problems
rows: Excess type III collagen in parallel bundles
Stays inside the wound edges, may regress
Excess disorganized type I and III collagen
Grows beyond the wound, earlobes, chest, shoulders, darker skin, recurs after excision
Bulges above the skin and blocks re-epithelialization
Wound splits open, often abdominal, from coughing, vomiting, or ileus
Deforming scar, common after burns over joints, palms, and soles

charts.title: Pressure injury stages
rows: Partial-thickness loss with exposed dermis or an intact or ruptured serum blister
Full-thickness skin loss with visible fat; no bone, tendon, or muscle
Full-thickness loss with exposed fascia, muscle, tendon, cartilage, or bone
Base hidden by slough or eschar

tricks.label: Three goes to one
tricks.text: Granulation tissue lays down type III collagen; remodeling swaps it for strong type I. A scar never gets back past about 80 percent of normal strength.

tricks.label: Keloid keeps going
tricks.text: A hypertrophic scar respects the wound border; a keloid crosses it. If the scar is bigger than the cut, think keloid.

tricks.label: Small hole, big damage
tricks.text: With electrical injury, judge the patient by the muscle and the urine, not by the size of the skin wound. Dark urine with a positive blood dipstick and few red cells suggests myoglobin.

highYield: Macrophages are the key cell of wound healing; neutrophils come first but macrophages drive repair from about day 3.
Vitamin C deficiency stops collagen hydroxylation, so wounds fail and old scars can reopen.
Full-thickness burns are painless because dermal nerve endings are destroyed.
Pseudomonas aeruginosa is the classic organism of burn wound sepsis.
Electrical injury causes rhabdomyolysis and myoglobinuric acute kidney injury.
Chronic radiation damage includes obliterative endarteritis, which starves tissue and stalls healing.
Cauliflower ear results from a hematoma separating perichondrium from avascular cartilage.
Brown recluse venom is sphingomyelinase D, causing a necrotic ulcer.
pitfalls: Superficial burns are left out of the rule of nines total; count only partial-thickness and full-thickness areas.
Painless burns are not mild; loss of pain means full-thickness destruction of nerves.
A stage 2 pressure injury is partial thickness; once fat shows it is at least stage 3.
Black widow venom (alpha-latrotoxin) is neurotoxic with muscle cramps; brown recluse venom causes skin necrosis.

dumps.p: Draw a timeline from the moment of a skin cut to one year later. Mark each phase, its main cells, and the main molecules.
l: Hemostasis: platelets, fibrin, PDGF and TGF-beta release
Neutrophils in the first 1 to 2 days
Macrophages dominate by about day 3
Granulation tissue: fibroblasts, VEGF-driven capillaries, type III collagen
Re-epithelialization from wound edges
Myofibroblast contraction, most in secondary intention
Remodeling: type III to type I collagen, zinc-dependent metalloproteinases
Strength reaches only about 70 to 80 percent of normal

dumps.p: Build a table comparing the four burn depths by layers involved, blisters, blanching, sensation, and healing. Then list the main complications of a large burn.
l: Superficial: epidermis, no blisters, painful, heals without scar
Superficial partial-thickness: blisters, blanches, very painful
Deep partial-thickness: blisters, poor blanching, reduced sensation, scars
Full-thickness: no blanching, painless, needs grafting
Hypovolemic burn shock from capillary leak
Pseudomonas sepsis
Hypermetabolism with muscle wasting
Inhalation injury, carbon monoxide, contractures

summary: The skin is an immune organ: keratinocytes, mast cells, and Langerhans cells sense danger and start both innate and adaptive responses. This unit links those responses to inflammation, granulomas, the four hypersensitivity types, autoimmune skin signs, tumor immunity, and vaccines.

points: Keratinocytes carry Toll-like receptors (TLR2 for gram-positive cell wall parts, TLR4 for LPS) and release IL-1 and TNF.
Keratinocytes secrete antimicrobial peptides: beta-defensins and cathelicidin (LL-37).
Mast cells sit beside dermal vessels and release histamine, TNF, and lipid mediators when triggered.
Langerhans cells (CD1a, langerin, Birbeck granules) catch antigen in the epidermis.
After capture they express CCR7, travel in afferent lymphatics to the regional node, and present peptide on MHC II (and MHC I) with B7 costimulation to prime naive T cells.
Arteriolar dilation (histamine, prostaglandins, nitric oxide) brings redness and heat.
Postcapillary venules leak (histamine, bradykinin, leukotrienes C4, D4, E4) causing edema.
Rolling: E-selectin and P-selectin on endothelium bind sialyl Lewis X on leukocytes.
Firm adhesion: leukocyte beta-2 integrins (LFA-1, Mac-1) bind ICAM-1 on endothelium.
Transmigration through the venule wall uses PECAM-1 (CD31).
Chemotaxis toward C5a, LTB4, IL-8, and bacterial peptides.
Leukocyte adhesion deficiency type 1: CD18 defect, very high blood neutrophils, infections without pus, poor wound healing, delayed umbilical cord separation.
Resolution when the cause is removed; macrophages clear dead neutrophils.
Abscess when pyogenic bacteria (S aureus) cause liquefactive necrosis walled off by granulation tissue.
Chronic inflammation when the cause persists: macrophages, lymphocytes, plasma cells, and fibrosis.
Granuloma: macrophages make IL-12, which drives Th1 cells; Th1 cells make IFN-gamma, which turns macrophages into epithelioid cells and giant cells; TNF keeps it intact.
Caseating granulomas: tuberculosis and some fungi. Noncaseating: sarcoidosis, Crohn disease, foreign bodies.
Lupus: photosensitive malar rash sparing nasolabial folds; discoid lesions scar and plug follicles.
Lupus skin biopsy: interface dermatitis with granular IgG, IgM, and C3 along the dermal-epidermal junction.
Dermatomyositis: Gottron papules over knuckles, heliotrope periorbital rash, proximal muscle weakness, raised cancer risk.
Systemic sclerosis: sclerodactyly and Raynaud; anticentromere in limited (CREST) disease, anti-Scl-70 (topoisomerase I) in diffuse disease with lung fibrosis.
CD8 T cells kill tumor cells showing mutant or viral peptides on MHC I; NK cells kill cells that have lost MHC I.
Tumors escape by dropping MHC I and by expressing PD-L1, which binds PD-1 and switches T cells off.
Transplant recipients on lifelong immunosuppression get many cutaneous squamous cell carcinomas, often outnumbering basal cell carcinomas.
HPV vaccine: recombinant L1 capsid protein self-assembles into virus-like particles with no DNA, inducing neutralizing IgG.
Live attenuated varicella vaccine replicates, so it induces antibody plus CD8 and CD4 T cell immunity.
Toxoid booster given to someone with high antitoxin IgG can cause an Arthus reaction: local immune complexes, complement, neutrophils, painful swelling within hours.

charts.title: Hypersensitivity in the skin
rows: Allergen cross-links IgE on mast cells; histamine, leukotrienes
Immune complexes in vessel walls activate complement, neutrophils
Arthus 4 to 12 hours; serum sickness 1 to 2 weeks
Sensitized T cells release cytokines or kill
Allergic contact dermatitis, tuberculin skin test

tricks.label: ACID
tricks.text: Hypersensitivity types I to IV: Anaphylactic and Atopic (I), Cytotoxic antibody (II), Immune complex (III), Delayed cell-mediated (IV).

tricks.label: CREST
tricks.text: Limited systemic sclerosis: Calcinosis, Raynaud phenomenon, Esophageal dysmotility, Sclerodactyly, Telangiectasia. Anticentromere antibody.

tricks.label: Roll, stick, squeeze, follow
tricks.text: Selectins roll, integrins stick to ICAM-1, PECAM-1 squeezes through, chemokines and C5a lead the way.

highYield: Langerhans cells carry skin antigen to regional lymph nodes and prime naive T cells.
LAD type 1 is a CD18 defect: neutrophilia, no pus, delayed umbilical cord separation.
IFN-gamma from Th1 cells activates macrophages to form granulomas; TNF maintains them.
Allergic contact dermatitis and the tuberculin test are type IV reactions peaking at 48 to 72 hours.
Lupus skin shows granular immune deposits at the dermal-epidermal junction.
Anti-Scl-70 marks diffuse systemic sclerosis; anticentromere marks limited disease.
Loss of MHC I hides tumors from CD8 T cells but exposes them to NK cells.
The HPV vaccine contains no viral DNA; it is L1 virus-like particles.
pitfalls: Pemphigus and bullous pemphigoid are antibody-mediated (type II); delayed T cell reactions are type IV.
LAD type 1 raises the blood neutrophil count; patients have many neutrophils that cannot leave the vessels.
An Arthus reaction is antibody and complement driven (type III), unlike a delayed T cell reaction (type IV), and it peaks within hours.
Dermatomyositis skin findings can appear before muscle weakness; screen for an underlying cancer.

dumps.p: Draw a postcapillary venule and a neutrophil leaving it. Label each step and the molecules on both cells.
l: Vasodilation and venular leak from histamine, bradykinin, leukotrienes
Margination of leukocytes to the wall
Rolling on E-selectin and P-selectin via sialyl Lewis X
Chemokines activate integrins
Firm adhesion of LFA-1 and Mac-1 (CD18) to ICAM-1
Transmigration with PECAM-1
Chemotaxis to C5a, LTB4, IL-8
LAD type 1: CD18 defect blocks firm adhesion

dumps.p: Build a table of the four hypersensitivity types with mechanism, key mediators, timing, and one skin example each.
l: Type I: IgE, mast cells, histamine, minutes, urticaria
Type II: IgG to fixed antigen, pemphigus and bullous pemphigoid
Type III: immune complexes, complement, neutrophils
Type III examples: Arthus reaction in hours, leukocytoclastic vasculitis
Type IV: T cells, cytokines, 48 to 72 hours
Type IV examples: contact dermatitis, tuberculin test
Only type IV is antibody independent

summary: The organisms behind common skin disease: staph and strep, dermatophytes and yeasts, the warts and pox viruses, the herpesviruses, and the vector-borne infections that show up first on the skin. The exam asks you to identify each from lab clues and to explain how its virulence factors make the disease.

points: Gram-positive cocci in clusters; catalase positive, coagulase positive.
Protein A binds the Fc end of IgG, blocking opsonization and complement.
Panton-Valentine leukocidin forms pores in leukocytes and is linked to necrotic community MRSA abscesses.
Exfoliative toxins cleave desmoglein 1; TSST-1 is a superantigen (toxic shock syndrome).
MRSA carries mecA, which encodes PBP2a, a penicillin-binding protein with low affinity for beta-lactams.
Gram-positive cocci in chains; beta-hemolytic, catalase negative, bacitracin sensitive, PYR positive.
M protein blocks complement deposition and phagocytosis; the hyaluronic acid capsule looks like host tissue and resists phagocytosis.
Streptolysin O lyses cells and is immunogenic (ASO titer); streptokinase turns plasminogen to plasmin and dissolves fibrin.
Pyrogenic exotoxins are superantigens: scarlet fever and streptococcal toxic shock.
Skin infection by nephritogenic strains can cause glomerulonephritis; rheumatic fever follows only pharyngitis, because the rheumatogenic M types are throat strains.
Dermatophytes (Trichophyton, Microsporum, Epidermophyton) make keratinases and live only in dead keratin: stratum corneum, hair, and nails.
KOH prep of scale shows branching septate hyphae.
Malassezia: lipophilic yeast; tinea versicolor gives hypopigmented or hyperpigmented scaly patches on the upper trunk.
Malassezia KOH prep: short hyphae with round yeasts (spaghetti and meatballs); its azelaic acid inhibits tyrosinase, causing pale spots.
Candida albicans: budding yeast and pseudohyphae; germ tube positive at 37 °C (98.6 °F).
Candida risks: moisture, diabetes, antibiotics that remove competing flora, glucocorticoids; T cell (Th17) defects cause mucocutaneous disease, neutropenia allows invasive disease.
HPV: nonenveloped, circular double-stranded DNA; infects basal keratinocytes through tiny breaks and replicates as cells mature upward.
Koilocytes: keratinocytes with a clear halo around a wrinkled nucleus.
High-risk HPV (16, 18): E6 sends p53 for degradation and E7 binds Rb, releasing E2F.
Molluscum contagiosum: poxvirus, enveloped double-stranded DNA that replicates in the cytoplasm; umbilicated papules with molluscum bodies (large eosinophilic cytoplasmic inclusions).
HSV-1, HSV-2, and VZV: enveloped double-stranded DNA; infect epithelium, travel up sensory axons, and stay latent in ganglia; reactivation gives herpes labialis, genital herpes, or dermatomal zoster.
Tzanck smear of a vesicle base shows multinucleated giant cells in both HSV and VZV.
Cutibacterium acnes: gram-positive anaerobic rod; lipases break sebum into irritating free fatty acids.
C acnes also activates TLR2 on monocytes and keratinocytes, releasing IL-1, IL-8, and IL-12 and drawing in neutrophils.
Pseudomonas aeruginosa: gram-negative rod, oxidase positive, non-lactose fermenter; grows in poorly chlorinated warm water.
Hot tub folliculitis: itchy follicular pustules in areas covered by a swimsuit, a day or two after exposure.

charts.title: Skin viruses compared
rows: Skin contact, fomites, sexual in adults
Multinucleated giant cells; latency in trigeminal or sacral ganglia
Multinucleated giant cells; latency in dorsal root and cranial ganglia

tricks.label: Coagulase sorts the staph
tricks.text: Coagulase positive means S aureus. Coagulase negative usually means S epidermidis, a skin resident that causes trouble mostly on catheters and implants.

tricks.label: Epidermophyton skips hair, Microsporum skips nails
tricks.text: Trichophyton hits skin, hair, and nails. Each of the other two skips one: Epidermophyton never hair, Microsporum never nails.

tricks.label: E6 for p53, E7 for Rb
tricks.text: Pair the numbers in order: 6 comes before 7, and p53 is named before Rb in the phrase 'p53 and Rb'.

highYield: mecA encodes PBP2a, the basis of MRSA beta-lactam resistance.
Protein A binds IgG Fc; M protein blocks complement; both defeat opsonization.
Group A strep skin infection can cause glomerulonephritis but not rheumatic fever.
Dermatophytes stay in dead keratin; KOH shows septate hyphae.
Tinea versicolor KOH: spaghetti and meatballs.
Candida forms pseudohyphae and is germ tube positive.
HSV-1 hides in the trigeminal ganglion, HSV-2 in sacral ganglia, VZV in dorsal root ganglia.
Rocky Mountain spotted fever rash moves from wrists and ankles inward to the trunk and involves palms and soles.
pitfalls: Tzanck smear cannot tell HSV from VZV; both show multinucleated giant cells.
Molluscum replicates in the cytoplasm, unlike most DNA viruses, because poxviruses carry their own RNA polymerase.
Tinea versicolor is caused by Malassezia, a yeast. Dermatophytes play no part despite the name.
Cutaneous larva migrans has no insect vector; larvae burrow directly into bare skin.

Skin strains can cause glomerulonephritis; rheumatic fever follows only pharyngitis

Virus enters sensory nerve endings
Retrograde axonal transport to the trigeminal ganglion (HSV-1)
Latency in the neuron nucleus with no virus production
Triggers: stress, fever, UV light, immunosuppression
Anterograde transport back to the same skin area
Tzanck smear shows multinucleated giant cells

summary: Pigment problems come from too many melanocytes, too much melanin, or missing melanocytes. This unit covers the common mole (nevocellular nevus) and vitiligo, and the look-alikes the exam uses as distractors: albinism, tinea versicolor, freckles, lentigines, melasma, and the bronze skin of Addison disease.

points: A benign tumor of melanocytes that grow in nests (nevus cells).
Starts with an activating BRAF (often V600E) or NRAS mutation that drives growth.
Growth then stops through oncogene-induced senescence, with p16 build-up holding the cells in arrest.
Nevi evolve with age: junctional in children, compound in young adults, intradermal in older adults.
Maturation with depth: superficial cells are larger, nested, and pigmented; deeper cells are smaller, less pigmented, and spindle shaped.
Loss of maturation with depth is a warning sign for melanoma.
Benign nevus: small, symmetric, sharp border, one even color, stable over time.
Melanoma warning signs follow ABCDE: asymmetry, irregular border, color variation, diameter over 6 mm, evolution.
A mole that looks different from the patient's other moles (ugly duckling) deserves a biopsy.
Large congenital melanocytic nevi carry a higher lifetime melanoma risk; small congenital nevi carry little added risk.
Autoimmune: CD8 T cells destroy melanocytes, driven by IFN-gamma signaling.
Sharply demarcated, milk-white depigmented macules, often symmetric around the mouth, eyes, hands, genitals, and bony points.
Wood lamp makes patches bright blue-white and easier to see.
Koebner phenomenon: new patches appear at sites of skin injury.
Biopsy: melanocytes absent from the basal layer.
Linked to autoimmune thyroid disease (most common), type 1 diabetes, pernicious anemia, and Addison disease.
Ephelides (freckles): normal number of melanocytes making more melanin; darken in summer and fade in winter.
Lentigo simplex: more melanocytes along the basal layer; does not darken with sun.
Solar lentigines: more basal melanocytes and melanin in chronically sun-exposed skin of older adults; they do not fade.
Melasma: symmetric brown patches on cheeks, forehead, and upper lip with pregnancy or estrogen; sun makes it worse.
Primary adrenal insufficiency lowers cortisol, removing feedback, so the pituitary makes much more POMC and ACTH.
ACTH and the MSH sequences cut from POMC stimulate melanocortin 1 receptors on melanocytes.
Result: diffuse hyperpigmentation, strongest in palmar creases, gums and buccal mucosa, scars, and sun-exposed skin.
Secondary adrenal insufficiency has low ACTH, so the skin does not darken.

rows: Dome-shaped, often skin-colored or light tan

rows: Normal number, little melanin (often tyrosinase defect)

charts.title: Brown spots compared

tricks.label: ABCDE
tricks.text: Melanoma warning signs: Asymmetry, Border irregularity, Color variation, Diameter over 6 mm, Evolution (change in size, shape, color, or symptoms).

tricks.label: Junction to dermis with age
tricks.text: Nevus cells drop from the junction into the dermis as a person ages: junctional (child), compound (young adult), intradermal (older adult).

tricks.label: Absent versus quiet
tricks.text: In vitiligo the melanocytes are gone. In albinism, tinea versicolor, and postinflammatory hypopigmentation they are present but make less melanin.

highYield: BRAF V600E is the most common driver mutation in common nevi.
Intradermal nevi have nests only in the dermis and are common in older adults.
Large congenital nevi raise melanoma risk.
Vitiligo: CD8 T cells destroy melanocytes; biopsy shows none.
Vitiligo is often seen with autoimmune thyroid disease.
Freckles have a normal number of melanocytes; lentigines have more.
Primary adrenal insufficiency darkens skin through high ACTH and POMC-derived MSH; secondary does not.
pitfalls: Vitiligo and albinism both look white; albinism is generalized from birth with eye findings and normal melanocyte numbers.
Tinea versicolor can be darker or lighter than surrounding skin; the fine scale and positive KOH settle it.
A uniform, small, flat dark mole in a child is most likely a junctional nevus; darkness alone does not mean melanoma.
Melasma follows pregnancy or estrogen; freckles follow sun exposure and fade.

dumps.p: Draw three skin cross sections side by side showing a junctional, a compound, and an intradermal nevus. Label where the nests sit and how the cells change with depth.
l: Junctional: nests at the dermal-epidermal junction, flat lesion
Compound: nests at the junction and in the dermis, raised lesion
Intradermal: nests in the dermis only, dome-shaped and often pale
Age progression from junctional to intradermal
Superficial cells larger, nested, pigmented
Deep cells smaller, less pigment, spindle shaped (maturation)
Start: BRAF or NRAS mutation; stop: oncogene-induced senescence

dumps.p: Make a table comparing vitiligo, albinism, tinea versicolor, and postinflammatory hypopigmentation by melanocytes, distribution, Wood lamp, KOH, and associations.
l: Vitiligo: melanocytes absent, CD8 T cell destruction
Vitiligo: bright Wood lamp accentuation, Koebner phenomenon
Vitiligo associations: autoimmune thyroid disease, type 1 diabetes
Albinism: normal melanocytes, defective melanin synthesis, generalized from birth
Tinea versicolor: Malassezia, upper trunk, fine scale, positive KOH
Postinflammatory: at sites of earlier inflammation, melanocytes present
Only vitiligo lacks melanocytes on biopsy

summary: Acute inflammatory rashes: atopic dermatitis, contact dermatitis, erythema multiforme, and urticaria, plus Stevens-Johnson syndrome, pityriasis rosea, seborrheic dermatitis, and aphthous ulcers. The exam wants the immune mechanism behind each rash and the clue in its distribution, timing, or histology that names it.

points: Filaggrin loss-of-function mutations weaken the stratum corneum, so water escapes and allergens and microbes get in.
Th2 inflammation follows: IL-4 and IL-13 drive IgE and further weaken the barrier; IL-31 drives itch.
Infants: face, scalp, and extensor surfaces. Older children and adults: flexures (elbow and knee creases, neck, wrists).
Chronic scratching thickens skin into lichenification.
Part of the atopic triad with allergic rhinitis and asthma.
Complications: S aureus colonization and infection, and eczema herpeticum (widespread HSV with punched-out erosions and fever).
Allergic: type IV. Small haptens (nickel, urushiol from poison ivy and oak) bind skin proteins and Langerhans cells sensitize T cells.
On re-exposure, memory T cells cause an itchy, vesicular eruption 48 to 72 hours later; patch test is positive.
Irritant: direct chemical or physical damage to keratinocytes (soaps, solvents, wet work); no sensitization needed and patch test is negative.
Shape follows exposure: earlobes, wrist, or belly button area from nickel; linear vesicles from plants; hands from wet work.
Histology of both, and of acute eczema: spongiosis (fluid between keratinocytes that stretches their junctions).
Erythema multiforme: cytotoxic T cells attack keratinocytes, most often after HSV, sometimes after Mycoplasma pneumoniae.
Target lesions with a dusky or blistered center on hands, feet, and extensor limbs; mucosa limited or spared.
Histology: interface dermatitis with lymphocytes at the junction and scattered necrotic keratinocytes.
Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis: drug-triggered CD8 T cell killing causes full-thickness epidermal necrosis.
SJS involves under 10 percent of body surface; TEN over 30 percent; 10 to 30 percent is overlap.
Painful dusky skin, mucosal involvement (usually two or more sites), positive Nikolsky sign; triggers include sulfonamides, anticonvulsants, and allopurinol.
Mast cells release histamine, causing edema in the superficial dermis: itchy wheals that each last under 24 hours.
Triggers: IgE (foods, drugs, stings), direct mast cell release (opioids, radiocontrast), physical (pressure, cold, heat, exercise).
Chronic urticaria lasts over 6 weeks; many cases involve IgG autoantibodies to IgE or its receptor.
Angioedema is the same leak in deeper dermis and subcutis: swelling of lips, eyelids, tongue, or airway.
Bradykinin angioedema has no hives and does not respond to antihistamines: hereditary C1 inhibitor deficiency (low C4) or ACE inhibitors.
Pityriasis rosea: a single herald patch, then oval scaly patches along skin cleavage lines (Christmas tree on the back); clears on its own in about 6 to 8 weeks.
Seborrheic dermatitis: inflammatory response to Malassezia in oily areas (scalp, eyebrows, nasolabial folds) with greasy yellow scale; cradle cap in infants; severe in HIV and Parkinson disease.
Aphthous ulcers: painful, shallow oral ulcers with a yellow-gray base and red halo on nonkeratinized mucosa; heal in 1 to 2 weeks.
Recurrent aphthous ulcers point toward Behçet disease, inflammatory bowel disease, or celiac disease.

tricks.label: Infants out, adults in
tricks.text: Atopic dermatitis starts on the outside of the limbs and the face in infants and moves into the creases (flexures) in older children and adults.

tricks.label: Draw the exposure
tricks.text: In contact dermatitis, the rash is a picture of what touched the skin: a watchband, an earring, a jeans snap, or a plant leaf dragged across the leg.

tricks.label: 10 and 30
tricks.text: Under 10 percent detached is SJS, over 30 percent is TEN, and between is overlap.

highYield: Filaggrin mutations cause the barrier defect in atopic dermatitis.
Eczema herpeticum is disseminated HSV in atopic skin.
Allergic contact dermatitis is type IV and appears 48 to 72 hours after re-exposure.
Spongiosis is the histologic hallmark of eczematous dermatitis.
HSV is the most common trigger of erythema multiforme.
Each urticarial wheal lasts under 24 hours; chronic urticaria lasts over 6 weeks.
Hereditary angioedema: low C1 inhibitor, low C4, no hives.
Sulfonamides, anticonvulsants, and allopurinol are classic SJS/TEN triggers.
pitfalls: Erythema multiforme is usually triggered by infection (HSV); SJS and TEN are usually triggered by drugs.
Irritant contact dermatitis needs no prior sensitization and has a negative patch test.
Angioedema without hives in a patient on an ACE inhibitor is bradykinin mediated; antihistamines will not help.
Pityriasis rosea can mimic secondary syphilis; palms and soles involvement points to syphilis.
Aphthous ulcers sit on movable, nonkeratinized mucosa; recurrent HSV inside the mouth favors keratinized hard palate and gums.

dumps.p: Draw the sensitization and elicitation phases of poison ivy dermatitis, from the first touch to the rash on a second exposure.
l: Urushiol is a hapten that binds skin proteins
Langerhans cells take up the hapten-protein complex
Langerhans cells migrate to the regional lymph node
Naive T cells are primed; first exposure gives no rash or a late mild one
Re-exposure: memory T cells home to the skin
Cytokines and cytotoxic T cells damage keratinocytes
Itchy linear vesicles 48 to 72 hours later
Spongiosis on biopsy; positive patch test

dumps.p: Build a table comparing atopic dermatitis, allergic contact dermatitis, erythema multiforme, urticaria, and SJS/TEN by trigger, immune mechanism, timing, and key skin finding.
l: Atopic dermatitis: filaggrin barrier defect plus Th2, chronic relapsing, flexural in adults
Allergic contact: type IV, 48 to 72 hours, distribution matches exposure
Erythema multiforme: HSV, cytotoxic T cells, acral target lesions
Urticaria: mast cells and histamine, wheals under 24 hours
SJS/TEN: drugs, CD8 T cells, full-thickness necrosis, mucosa involved
SJS under 10 percent, TEN over 30 percent
Bradykinin angioedema has no hives
